title: Your first SELECT
concept: A database stores information in tables – like spreadsheets with rows and named columns. SELECT asks the database to show you data, and FROM says which table to read. The star * means “every column”.
why: Every data job starts by looking at the data. SELECT is the most used SQL command in the world.
example_note: Returns every column and every row of the employees table.
prompt: Show all columns and all rows from the departments table.
hints: Use SELECT * to pick every column.
The table name goes after FROM.
SELECT * FROM departments;

title: Choosing columns
concept: Instead of * you can list the exact columns you want, separated by commas. You can also rename a column in the output with AS.
why: Real tables have dozens of columns. Selecting only what you need makes results readable and faster.
example_sql:
SELECT name, job_title AS role
FROM employees;
example_note: Two columns only; job_title is displayed as “role”.
prompt: Show the name and salary of every employee.
hints: List the columns after SELECT, separated by a comma.
SELECT name, salary FROM employees;

title: Filtering with WHERE
concept: WHERE keeps only the rows that match a condition. Compare with =, >, <, >=, <= or <> (not equal). Text values go in single quotes.
why: Nobody wants all the data – they want the customers in Spain or the orders over $500. WHERE is how you ask.
example_note: Only customers whose country is exactly USA.
prompt: Show the name and salary of employees who earn more than 90000.
starter:
SELECT name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE
solution: SELECT name, salary FROM employees WHERE salary > 90000;
hints: Use the > operator – no quotes around numbers.
WHERE salary > 90000

title: AND, OR, IN & LIKE
concept: Combine conditions with AND (both true) and OR (either true). IN (…) checks a list of values and LIKE matches text patterns, where % means “anything”.
why: Real questions have several conditions: “Furniture or Stationery, and cheap”.
example_note: Customers from USA or Spain, or whose name starts with M.
prompt: Show name, category and price of products in the Furniture or Stationery categories that cost less than 100.
starter:
SELECT name, category, price
FROM products
WHERE
solution: SELECT name, category, price FROM products WHERE category IN ('Furniture','Stationery') AND price < 100;
hints: category IN ('Furniture', 'Stationery') handles the first condition.
Join it to price < 100 with AND.

title: Sorting with ORDER BY
concept: ORDER BY sorts the result. The default is ascending (ASC); add DESC for largest-first. You can sort by several columns.
why: Leaderboards, “newest first”, “cheapest first” – sorted output is everywhere.
prompt: Show name and salary of all employees, highest salary first.
starter:
SELECT name, salary
FROM employees
ORDER BY
solution: SELECT name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC;
hints: ORDER BY salary …
Add DESC after the column for highest first.

title: LIMIT & DISTINCT
concept: LIMIT n returns only the first n rows – combine it with ORDER BY for “top 3” style questions. DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from the output.
why: “Top 10 products” and “which countries do we sell to?” are classic reporting questions.
prompt: Show the name and price of the 3 most expensive products, most expensive first.
solution: SELECT name, price FROM products ORDER BY price DESC LIMIT 3;
hints: Sort by price descending first.
Then add LIMIT 3 at the very end.

title: Aggregate functions
concept: Aggregate functions turn many rows into one value: COUNT(), SUM(), AVG(), MIN(), MAX(). COUNT(*) counts rows.
why: Totals, averages and counts are the numbers on every business dashboard.
example_sql:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS products, MAX(price) AS priciest
FROM products;
example_note: One row: how many products, and the highest price.
prompt: In one row, show the number of employees and their average salary (two columns).
solution: SELECT COUNT(*) AS total, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary FROM employees;
hints: COUNT(*) counts rows.
AVG(salary) gives the average.
SELECT COUNT(*), AVG(salary) FROM employees;

title: GROUP BY
concept: GROUP BY splits rows into groups and runs the aggregate on each group separately. Every non-aggregated column in SELECT must appear in GROUP BY.
why: “Sales per region”, “orders per customer” – any “per” question is a GROUP BY.
example_note: One row per status with its order count.
prompt: For each product category, show the category and the number of products in it.
solution: SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS products FROM products GROUP BY category;
hints: COUNT(*) gives the number per group.
Finish with GROUP BY category.

title: HAVING
concept: WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after aggregation – use it when the condition involves COUNT, SUM, AVG…
why: Lets you ask “which customers placed more than 3 orders?”
example_sql:
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;
example_note: Only customers with 3 or more orders.
prompt: Show each department_id from employees together with its employee count, but only departments with more than 2 employees.
starter:
SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) AS headcount
FROM employees
GROUP BY department_id
solution: SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) AS headcount FROM employees GROUP BY department_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 2;
hints: The condition is on COUNT(*), so WHERE will not work.
HAVING COUNT(*) > 2

title: INNER JOIN
concept: Data lives in separate tables linked by keys. JOIN … ON matches rows from two tables, for example employees.department_id = departments.id. Use table aliases (e, d) to keep queries short.
why: Relational databases split data to avoid repetition. JOINs put it back together for answers.
example_note: Each employee next to their department name.
prompt: Show each employee's name together with their department name and department location.
starter:
SELECT e.name, 
FROM employees e
JOIN
solution: SELECT e.name, d.name, d.location FROM employees e JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.department_id;
hints: JOIN departments d ON … links the two tables.
The link is d.id = e.department_id.

title: LEFT JOIN
concept: LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table, even with no match – the missing side is NULL. Test for it with IS NULL (never = NULL).
why: Finding what is missing – customers who never ordered – is a core analyst skill.
example_note: Customers with no orders show NULL under order_id.
prompt: Show the name of customers who have never placed an order.
starter:
SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE
solution: SELECT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL;
hints: A customer with no orders has NULL in every orders column.
WHERE o.id IS NULL

title: Subqueries
concept: A subquery is a query inside another query, wrapped in parentheses. It is often used in WHERE to compare against a calculated value.
why: Lets you ask two-step questions in one statement: “who earns more than the average?”
example_sql:
SELECT name, price FROM products
WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products);
example_note: Products priced above the overall average.
prompt: Show name and salary of employees who earn more than the average salary.
starter:
SELECT name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary > (
solution: SELECT name, salary FROM employees WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees);
hints: The inner query is just SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees.
Close the parenthesis and end with ;

title: CASE expressions
concept: CASE WHEN … THEN … ELSE … END is SQL's if/else. It creates a new, labelled value for every row.
why: Turns raw numbers into categories – “High / Medium / Low” – for reports.
example_note: Adds a tier label to each product.
prompt: Show employee name and a column band: 'High' if salary ≥ 90000, 'Mid' if salary ≥ 60000, otherwise 'Entry'.
starter:
SELECT name,
  CASE
    WHEN 
  END AS band
FROM employees;
solution: SELECT name, CASE WHEN salary >= 90000 THEN 'High' WHEN salary >= 60000 THEN 'Mid' ELSE 'Entry' END AS band FROM employees;
hints: Check the highest threshold first – CASE stops at the first match.
WHEN salary >= 90000 THEN 'High' WHEN salary >= 60000 THEN 'Mid' ELSE 'Entry'

title: Common Table Expressions
concept: A CTE (WITH name AS (…)) gives a query a temporary name so later queries can reuse it. It breaks big problems into readable steps.
why: Professional SQL is written in small named steps, not one giant nested query.
prompt: An order's total is quantity × price. Using a CTE called order_totals (columns id and total), show orders with a total above 500.
starter:
WITH order_totals AS (
  SELECT o.id, o.quantity * p.price AS total
  FROM orders o
  JOIN products p ON p.id = o.product_id
)
SELECT
solution: WITH order_totals AS (SELECT o.id, o.quantity * p.price AS total FROM orders o JOIN products p ON p.id = o.product_id) SELECT id, total FROM order_totals WHERE total > 500;
hints: The CTE is already written – just query it like a table.
SELECT id, total FROM order_totals WHERE total > 500;

title: Window functions
concept: A window function calculates across related rows without collapsing them. RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY … ORDER BY …) numbers rows inside each group.
why: Rankings, running totals and “top N per group” are impossible with plain GROUP BY.
example_note: Most expensive product in each category gets rank 1.
prompt: Show name, department_id, salary and a column dept_rank ranking employees by salary (highest = 1) within their department.
solution: SELECT name, department_id, salary, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dept_rank FROM employees;
hints: PARTITION BY restarts the ranking for each department.
PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC

title: INSERT
concept: INSERT INTO table (columns) VALUES (values) adds a new row. Always list the columns so the order is explicit. The primary key id is generated automatically if you leave it out.
why: Applications constantly add new users, orders and records.
example_sql:
INSERT INTO customers (name, city, country)
VALUES ('Sam Lee', 'Seoul', 'Korea');
example_note: Adds one customer. Use Run to try it – Reset restores the data.
prompt: Insert a new product: name 'Webcam', category 'Electronics', price 59, stock 40.
starter:
INSERT INTO products (name, category, price, stock)
VALUES (
solution: INSERT INTO products (name, category, price, stock) VALUES ('Webcam','Electronics',59,40);
verify: SELECT name, category, price, stock FROM products WHERE name = 'Webcam';
hints: Values must follow the same order as the column list.
VALUES ('Webcam', 'Electronics', 59, 40);

title: UPDATE & DELETE
concept: UPDATE … SET … WHERE … changes existing rows and DELETE FROM … WHERE … removes them. Always include WHERE – without it every row is affected!
why: Forgetting WHERE is the most famous SQL mistake. Learn the safe habit now: write SELECT with the same WHERE first.
prompt: Give every Engineering employee (department_id = 1) a 10% raise, then delete all cancelled orders. Run both statements.
solution: UPDATE employees SET salary = salary * 1.10 WHERE department_id = 1; DELETE FROM orders WHERE status = 'cancelled';
verify: SELECT (SELECT SUM(salary) FROM employees) AS payroll, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders) AS orders_left;
hints: salary = salary * 1.10 raises by 10%.
DELETE FROM orders WHERE status = 'cancelled';
